title: Houston in the 1930s as a country town
summary: Talk of Houston as a small place then, with his mother predicting it would become a great Southern city, and where on Nance Street he lived.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: But I just want to ask you something about Houston at that time. We're talking of what? 1930?
In the '30s.
Yeah. Well, I mean, Houston was a much smaller city then because, you know --
Houston was a country town.
It was, yeah.
But I didn't know it until later because I wasn't smart enough to know it. I was too young.
All right, but you had street cars. So now you take 50 lessons on the violin.
Yes, sir. And get back to Houston, my mother used to say the country (unintelligible), she said this is going to be one of the greatest metropolitan cities of the South. My mother said that.
Why did she say that?
Why did she think that?

I don't know. My mother lived in New York and ride the subway and people thought she had a sixth sense and she wouldn't bother nobody and they'd come over and ask her to tell them about themselves. She said, 'I don't know nothing about you.' But what she visualized was her

SITUATION.
(unintelligible).
I mean the big development of Houston has been since World War II, hasn't it really?

I wasn't here. I tell you what my mother says, Stan, and I want you to hear this, and I want you to look at Houston today, you can, and I think about what she said. She didn't pass until '75. She got to see some of it. But her predictions were very good, and she's no Nancy Dixon, I don't think. (Jeanne Dixon--ed.)
Well, when you lived on Nance Street, was that sort of in the city or was that getting out a bit?
What is that, now?
When you lived on Nance Street -
No. I was in the city.
Oh, it was in the city?
I was only ten minutes from town.
